related_questions.question: Will CD rates go up when the Fed raises interest rates?

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, CD interest rates tend to rise when the Federal Reserve raises the federal funds rate. This is because the Fed's actions influence other interest rates, including those offered on savings accounts and CDs.
snippet_highlighted_words: Yes, CD interest rates tend to rise when the Federal Reserve raises the federal funds rate

list.title: Federal Reserve Influence:
list.snippet: The Federal Reserve's main tool for influencing the economy is the federal funds rate, which is the interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. When the Fed raises this rate, it becomes more expensive for banks to borrow money, and they often pass those higher costs on to consumers through higher interest rates on savings accounts and CDs.

list.title: CDs and Savings Accounts:
list.snippet: Banks and credit unions use the federal funds rate as a benchmark when setting interest rates on deposit products like CDs.

list.title: Potential for Higher Rates:
list.snippet: If the Fed raises interest rates, you can expect to see banks and credit unions offering higher interest rates on their CDs, making them more attractive to savers.

list.title: Considerations for Savers:
list.snippet: If you are looking to open a CD, you may want to consider opening a short-term CD to take advantage of potentially higher rates in the future if the Fed continues to raise rates. You could also consider a CD ladder strategy, which involves investing in CDs with different maturity dates to balance earning potential with access to your funds.

list.title: Other Factors:
list.snippet: While the Fed's actions are a key factor, other elements like inflation and competition among banks can also influence CD rates.

text_blocks.snippet: In essence, when the Fed raises interest rates, it signals to financial institutions to offer higher yields on savings products like CDs, potentially leading to better returns for savers.

text_blocks.snippet: The Federal Reserve (also known as the Fed) doesn't have a fixed schedule for raising interest rates. Rate decisions are made at scheduled meetings of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). The FOMC typically meets eight times a year to review the economy and make decisions about the federal funds rate.
snippet_highlighted_words: doesn't have a fixed schedule for raising interest rates

list.title: Economic growth:
list.snippet: If the economy is growing too quickly, potentially leading to inflation, the Fed may raise interest rates to cool things down.

list.title: Inflation:
list.snippet: When inflation is high, the Fed is more likely to raise rates to reduce the purchasing power of money and slow down price increases.

list.title: Employment:
list.snippet: The Fed also considers the unemployment rate and the overall health of the labor market when making interest rate decisions.

list.title: Global economic conditions:
list.snippet: Events in other countries can also impact the U.S. economy and influence the Fed's decisions.
In 2022 and 2023, the Fed aggressively raised interest rates to combat high inflation.
In late 2024, the Fed started to slow down the pace of rate hikes and even began cutting rates as inflation started to cool down.
The current federal funds rate is in the range of 4.25% to 4.50%.
The Fed's decisions are closely watched by investors, businesses, and consumers, as they can have a significant impact on borrowing costs, investment decisions, and overall economic activity.
The next FOMC meeting is scheduled for July 29-30.
Additional meetings are scheduled for September 16-17, October 28-29, and December 9-10.
The exact date of the rate announcement is usually 2 p.m. EST on the second day of the meeting, followed by a press conference with the Federal Reserve Chair.
